utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those two vehicles after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Both vehicles were requisitioned. The van was turned into an ambulance, because there was a shortage of ambulance vehicles, and my personal vehicle was used by the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You said that these were the events of April 1993. When did you come back to the town of Vitez after these events?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was two months later. When my van had been taken, I was -- I became the driver of that vehicle, and so I spent there two months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were an ambulance driver for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, do you remember an incident which took place sometime in the middle of 1993, when, together with some other people, you travelled in a vehicle to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time I had gone to Vitez. I was with two friends -- actually, three friends, and the fourth was my wife's brother. We were driving from Nadioci in the direction of Vitez, and in the area called Buhine Kuce, between Kaonik and Vitez, my wife's brother was hit by a sniper. His name was Zarko Malenica, and he was wounded. And my friend, Zoran Mravak, who was sitting next to me, was wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not hit at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, I was not, but my wife's brother died on the way to being given help.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, I'm sorry that this happened to you, but I have to press you on it with one more question. Could you determine who shot at your vehicle and from where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was very simple to determine, because that was the most critical spot for the passage, and from a sniper -- there was a sniper active there almost permanently, from hour to hour, sometimes minute to minute, and those were positions held by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, what happened to your restaurant, the restaurant Kamin, during these hostilities in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: During the conflict my restaurant was completely demolished from the shelling of the town, so it was completely demolished and we had to completely renovate it when we restarted business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on you remodelled it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just clarify one matter, Mr. Jukic. You said that the vehicle in which you were travelling with the late Zarko Malenica, that you were shot at near the village of Buhine Kuce?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What military force was in that village? Who held that village?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was ABiH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last topic, Mr. Jukic, it concerns my client, Mr. Mario Cerkez. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I know him as a citizen of Vitez, who was a very correct man from an honest, working-class family. I have never heard anything bad about him, that he had any bad inclinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also patronise your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite often, and he was always a welcome guest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he was in your restaurant, have you ever heard him say anything derogatory about Muslims or Serbs, that he was a chauvinist of any sort?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard anything like that. I wasn't paying much attention to these things, but I don't believe he would have ever had such an attitude. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, do you know what position Mr. Cerkez held at the time with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time he was the commander of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that he had a position, but I wasn't well versed in those matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever had an opportunity to visit him in the place where he was working?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Jukic. That concludes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Mr. Kordic has no questions of this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few questions for you, Mr. Jukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you do, I understand you want to raise a matter ex parte. If there's time, at 4.00, depending on progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, just a few general matters, and indeed not so very many questions for you altogether, I don't think. First of all, your name. It may seem a silly question to start with, but is your name a common and frequently heard name in your territory or is it an unusual name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Slavko Jukic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand the question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there many men in your area with the name Slavko Jukic, or to your knowledge are you the only one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, now I'm the only one called Slavko Jukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I won't take long with this, but General Blaskic, or Colonel Blaskic as he was, at one time in his evidence spoke of a deputy chief of the civilian police called Slavko Jukic. Were you aware of anybody by that name?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the unit called the Vitezovi, the Knights, I think, sometimes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you help with anybody by the name of Slavko Jukic being in the Vitezovi or in the Knights in April of 1993? Is it your family or what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. I don't have any namesake in my family, nor do I know who that man could have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of your evidence very briefly. You live in Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from the time when you were away from Nadioci on the Kuber feature, have you basically spent every night of your life living at your address in Nadioci, your recent life?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't spend every night at this address, because we were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: On Kuber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from those nights when you were on Kuber, you were at home in Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you must have become aware of the establishment at what's been called the Bungalow at Nadioci, the establishment there of the military police unit called the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I knew nothing about it, because I'd only come in the evening, late in the evening, to have a rest, have some sleep, and then report once again in the morning. So I didn't know anything. I know there were some troops there, but I don't know who they were, what their name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with the incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Jukic, do you really mean to say that nobody talked in the village about the Jokers being in the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody talked, but I didn't. And I did not hear anything. I know there were some soldiers there, but I didn't know their name was Jokers or some other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the Bungalow was a restaurant, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a motel, but it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it now? What's happening there now?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: There is nothing there at the moment because there is a landslide there. Land slid to the place where the Bungalow was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how long were the soldiers in the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, three or four months, something like that. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And nobody said to you it's the Jokers who are in the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I repeat, I really didn't know, nor do I know that there were any troops there. That is, I knew that there were some troops there but I didn't know which and I didn't know whether they were Jokers or perhaps some other unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to give us an idea of the geographical intimacy of the area that we are dealing with, how near is Ahmici to Nadioci, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: It's about four kilometres, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As much as that or do you think it may be rather less?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I think that's about it, but I never measured it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just look at, just to remind the Judges, Exhibit 2624 will do. If you would just lie it on the ELMO. If the usher would be so good and focus on the area just above the "2" there, please. Just give us an idea. While this is coming your way and while the map is being prepared, Nadioci itself is a what, a village with a shop or without a shop, a village with a mosque or without a mosque? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Nadioci? Nadioci, well, that's a village. It has a shop. It doesn't have a mosque. And that's about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the booth could very kindly just focus down on Nadioci which is above the figure 2, and bring the village of Ahmici into focus. There it is, just above it. These places, Ahmici, Nadioci, they are all very close together, aren't they? They are all in sight of each other across the very low hills; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you can't see Ahmici from Nadioci or at least as far as I could see, one cannot see it. I'm telling you it can't be more than four kilometres. It is a fact that if one goes to Nadioci to Vitez, one has to go through Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to the map so perhaps we can just leave it on the ELMO for a minute, or I may come back to the map. I want to deal very briefly with the incident in January. Your restaurant was attacked. You don't know one way or another, yourself, who did it, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: It wasn't attacked. That was an explosive device which was placed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know one way or another who did it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know 100 per cent, but I received the information from the gentleman who said that it was an extremist group of the BH army which had placed it, and that they overheard a conversation between Mr. Sulejman Kalco and a commander, I can't remember who. But that's what he said, "That Kamim was a done job and that those guys did their job well."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever play you this tape? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't competent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a written report into this crime by Mr. Mirko Samija?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Mirko Samija still alive and well and able to give evidence so far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Lamentably, Mirko Samija was also killed at Buhine Kuce by a sniper acting from a stronghold of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But any report that was prepared into this attack, that would still exist in the archives of the police station presumably?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: All I know is that the police, the civilian police had come out to the scene of the crime but whether there is any record, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- on your account, you had done nothing to cause upset amongst any of the groups who might have been involved, whether they were Croats, Muslims, or anybody else, they all used your cafe, your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They frequented it. Everybody came to it and that is why I was so surprised by what had happened. I did not insist much because at that time, it wasn't really particularly wise to insist on finding out who had done it to me. And at that time, I didn't really care much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from what you were apparently told by someone in the police, this could have been simply a criminal act, and it certainly could have been an act by the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade who were going around the area committing criminal acts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: The information that it had been done by the extremist group of the BH army, I did not get it from anybody. I got it from the police commander, Mr. Samija, and I therefore do not think that Ludvig Pavlovic could have done that or why would they do something like that to me? They had no reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us in your statement -- I think you were telling us that rumours were spread that they were committing quite a lot of incidents in the area at the time. They were damaging properties, mostly Muslim, but also Croat properties. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I said that I had heard that the Novi Travnik -- that they had destroyed a few businesses, but I never said that they destroyed houses. I never heard anything about that. As I told you, I had no trouble with them because a couple of times they came to have lunch at my place so that -- and the relationship was a very correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble the witness with 2.8 in the summary, but the Chamber can see what's there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Now, you've given a date for when you say you were told of an attack by the ABiH in Kuber. I want some answers from you on that, please. Were you told about the attack on Kuber on the same day that it happened or did you only learn about it later?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: About the attack, I learned on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you when you learned about this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I was in my restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon, sometime around 5.00 or 6.00, that is 1700 or 1800.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Nobody told me directly but there were other people, villagers, that is local people from Vitez, and they were talking and said, well, we've heard that this and that had happened. And since the town was completely deserted, one could assume that they were telling the truth. But nobody told me directly about it. It is a fact that it transpired later on that it was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand you correctly. You were simply hearing other peoples' conversations and they were passing some rumours about something; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it from those people, but they -- it was no rumour; it was the truth, because they must have heard it from people, from reliable people, people in the know. I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the map again, although it may not be shown on this map. It doesn't matter. Kuber lies between Nadioci and Santici, lies to the north of those villages and between them and Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Kuber was the front line between Zenica towards Nadioci, Kratine and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, we've heard a lot of evidence -- I'm not going to weary you with all of this -- but we've heard a lot of evidence about what was happening in Vitez on the 15th of April, and I'm going to ask you this: Is what you're telling us about the 15th of April something that you've, in some way, reconstructed and in fact -- I'm sorry, what you're telling us about Kuber is something that you've reconstructed and that Kuber, in fact, was only involved in active fighting a day or so later than the 15th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Kuber was only the subject of active fighting a day or so after the 15th, no question of it being attacked on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there was an attack, but I know that that incident or whether the attack began then, I don't know. But it is a fact that I know when the attack began from Zenica towards Vitez via Kuber, and I think I'm sure it was on the 15th because they jointly held the front line against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you for your consideration that on the 15th, although the HVO was shutting Vitez down and closing it off towards the end of the day, there was no anxiety at that stage about attacks by the ABiH, and what was happening was preparation for defence for attacks on various villages including Ahmici near to you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have a feeling that the HVO closed the town because various coffee shops and restaurants were open late into the evening. I told you that I closed down my restaurant because my village was directly below the front line on Kuber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, whatever night it was or whatever day it was that you first heard about Kuber, you had spent the previous night at home and you had spent the night before that at home because you were living at home at that time; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your village, Nadioci, as we can see from this map, is extremely small; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are about a hundred households.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware, at any stage, in your village, before the night when you heard of what you say was an attack at Kuber, were you aware in your village of anything unusual happening on the night before or on two nights before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No. Everything was in order in the village. People lived their normal lives, worked. And when I -- when we came home, I didn't even want to talk about it, what I had heard or what I had seen. I simply didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you heard His Honour, the Presiding Judge, has asked you about the Bungalow. If, for example, there had suddenly been a lot of additional forces arriving at the Bungalow and heavy artillery or something of that sort, you would have seen it and it would have been talked about in your village. That must be right, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I could not see that evening when I came home, because there were no troops in the Bungalow then. After that I never passed that way. I didn't go to Vitez. It was on the way to Vitez, some 300 or 400 metres from my house, so that I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that answer in just a second, but equally, if in the night or the two nights before you learnt of the incident at Kuber there had been something as extraordinary as the arrival of Muslim soldiers in your village, you would have heard about it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If, on the night before the 15th, as you say it is, or the night before that, there had been something as extraordinary as a build-up of Muslim forces in your village, you would have heard about it; it's quite inevitable that you would have heard of such a thing happening, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that I would have heard, but I'm telling you that there were no troops that night, as far as I can remember. As far as I can remember, there were no troops in the Bungalow before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not just in the Bungalow. I'm talking now specifically about Muslim troops. There were no Muslim troops in your village on the night or nights before what you say was the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, there were none, because 98 per cent of my village is Croat, so that something like that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to go through the exercise of wearying the witness with a document that there's no reason to believe he would have seen, but the questions I've asked relate to an Exhibit 660.1. And it may be that you'll allow me, after the witness has withdrawn, just to explain the purpose of the question so that I can achieve that objective without going through the exercise with the witness and taking time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I return to the answer you gave not so very long ago about there being no soldiers in the Bungalow that night. Are you saying that there were no soldiers in the Bungalow the night when you returned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned from the town home, when we closed down, I did not see any soldiers in the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So although the map isn't entirely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although the map isn't entirely clear, the Bungalow, or the site of the Bungalow, is along the road coming from Vitez, passing the road to Ahmici and then passing Nadioci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may be wrong; correct me if I am. Look at the map. Is it indeed the case that where we see -- do you see to the left of the figure 2, there's a zero? Don't worry about that. It's got nothing to do with your evidence. We see to the left of that there's a curve in the road. Was the Bungalow somewhere in that area?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I really am not able to read the map. But it was some 300 or 400 metres from my house, in the direction of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your house was not on the main road; it was up in the hinterland, up in the fields, or where?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, not on the road itself, but ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the night of the 15th and in the morning of the 16th, you were at home when Ahmici was attacked. So what can you tell us, please, about that attack?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about the attack. All I know is that I had to go to the defence front line because our -- what we called it, our village guards, had been attacked from Kuber. And about this attack, I could not see it and I couldn't hear it at the time. Later on we heard that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It must be my mistake in reading your summary. You went home, according to your summary, on the evening of the 15th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak in your summary of there being a general mobilisation sometime in the evening of the 16th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was sometime in the evening of the 16th, according to your summary, that you registered as a Home Guard in the HVO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the morning, I went there, and the mobilisation was announced in the afternoon, because there had been a major attack by the BH army from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went where on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: On the 16th I went --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I went to the front line, up there, where my neighbours were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you register as a Home Guard, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't register anywhere. I simply went to the defence line to help my neighbours, because it was only the villagers of Nadioci there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Again I'm just using your summary. There are always problems with translations from your own language to English, but your summary says, "I registered as a Home Guard in the HVO." You told us that you went somewhere, a couple of questions ago, and I mistakenly thought you were indicating you went somewhere to register. What formalities did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you go through to become a Home Guard in the HVO, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment one could not register anywhere. It was self-organisation. And I do not know that anyone could register anywhere, because we simply -- we ourselves thought that we, as the Home Guards, were needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the morning of the 16th. You hadn't gone off as a Home Guard by then. Sometime in the course, your evidence is, I think, of the 16th that you went off. So please tell us about the attack on Ahmici. And if you'd look at the map, please, I can perhaps assist you. The start of the Ahmici attack was signalled, was it not, by the firing of a piece of artillery from the hill called Hrasno which we can see. If we look on this map, which I think is kilometre squares, but I might be wrong -- I'll have to be corrected -- which would be no more than a kilometre from you, in the same way as if I'm right about their being kilometre squares, Ahmici is a few hundred metres from you. I'm going to suggest to you that the Ahmici attack was signalled by artillery firing from Hrasno. Now, do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I do not know that it happened that way, because from Nadioci, yes, we can see Hrasno up there, but we cannot see Ahmici. And it was afterwards, when I climbed up to the front line, we could see that something was afoot there, that a couple of houses were in flames. As for where it started, how, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This attack on Ahmici started from, or parts of it started from that Bungalow a few hundred metres from where you lived. Are you really telling us that you have absolutely no knowledge of what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: I guarantee in full that I did not know whether it started from the Bungalow or where. I'm telling you: I didn't even know that it existed, and it was only two or three days later that we heard that yes, there were some troops in the Bungalow, but I really do not know whose soldiers were there, because -- I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that I followed this. Are you saying that you weren't woken by the fire at half past 5.00 in the morning; you just slept through it? What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of that, yes. One could hear some shots, and that is why that morning I went to the line, to my neighbour's, to see what was going on, and if need be, to lend them a hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it didn't occur to you to go down the road to see what was happening on the main road where the soldiers might be, soldiers who would, of course, be Croats and therefore likely to be receptive to you? It didn't occur to you to go down there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Never, ever did I think of that. Nothing prompted me to do that. I just dressed and went to the line on Kuber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, please: Your father's first name is what?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Niko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jukic, my friend has shown you the map which is to the left of you, showing the villages of Nadioci and Ahmici. Tell us: Can one village be seen from the other, in view of the relief of the ground?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You mean from the defence line?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'll repeat the question. You are an inhabitant of Nadioci, you told us. From the village of Nadioci, can you see the village of Ahmici, and why, if not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO JUKIC
utterances.text: No, you can't, because there is a big hill in between, and forest, because the village of Nadioci is in a valley or -- what do you call it? -- when compared to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jukic. I do not have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Jukic. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. We'll have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just while the next witness is coming in, may I, with your leave, explain what it is always possible to do in somewhat laborious cross-examination with a witness, but seems to be best avoid with the witness, on his own testimony, would have no knowledge of the particular document on which you would be inviting his comment. As I understand it at the moment, the Exhibit 660.1 is the only document of a contemporaneous type, if genuine, which refers to anything happening at Kuber in the regard spoken of by the witness as early as the 15th of April. All other documents -- again, no point in putting them to the witness -- fit with later dates. That same document which has been challenged by a witness as to its authenticity contains references to the build-up of Muslim forces in Nadioci on the night or so before the 15th, which was the purpose of the questions which I was asking of this witness, aimed at showing the falsity of that document, which was a Blaskic exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that we should argue on that matter now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It was an indulgence to allow Mr. Nice to explain. However, he's done so. I expect many of us remember the document. Yes. Now, your next witness, I take it, is Major Sajevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Sajevic. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sajevic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just relax, please. We know that you are in an environment that you are not familiar with, but please do relax. You live in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your address is Hrvatskih Branitelja, Croatian Defenders Street 7B, Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, after I put a question to you, make a short break so that we would give the interpreters enough time to interpret what we are saying because most of the people here do not speak our language. The address that you live at nowadays is -- it's actually an apartment building, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are quite a few such buildings in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born on the 26th of December 1956 in Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are married and you have two children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got a degree in science and mathematics in Sarajevo in 1981; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the former Yugoslavia you served in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended reserve officers' school there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: This was in a small town by the name of Bileca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bileca, that is where one of the biggest if not the biggest schools for reserve officers in the former Yugoslavia was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you left the Yugoslav People's Army with the rank of 2nd Lieutenant as a reservist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sajevic, does everybody get that rank automatically as soon as they finish that school?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of those who successfully completed the school, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you got a job; is that correct, when you returned to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your first job was in the municipal headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez, right, or did you work somewhere else before that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: My first job was in the secondary school before I went to do my military service. After I did my military service, I started working in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until this unfortunate war that we are discussing here started, you worked in the Territorial Defence headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you worked in the Territorial Defence, you acquired additional knowledge about this particular work, you attended seminars, exercises, training courses, et cetera. Could you tell us about this in a few words?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, all military conscripts who complete reserve officers' school are not at such a high level of military training in order to be in a position to work independently. They are further educated and trained on the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the Territorial Defence, you attended various exercises, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did you spend in the Territorial Defence altogether?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence, I was there from 1983 until the moment I walked out of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for at least nine years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an employee of this organisation, were you devoted in your heart to this organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, basically, yes. I can say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did your job professionally and honestly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your knowledge concerning the defence system that existed in Yugoslavia and in view of the fact that more or less the entire concept was taken over later by all the armed forces after Yugoslavia fell apart, I would like to put a few questions to you in this regard. The armed forces of the former Yugoslavia had two components. Which were these two basic components of Yugoslavia's defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: The two basic components of the defence of the former Yugoslavia were the JNA, that is to say, the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and the TO, the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, a certain role in the organisation of defence was placed by the civilian authorities, by the civilian factor. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: The civilian factor in this system, so to speak, were Secretariats of National Defence that were attached to municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what was the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in charge of. What duties did they have within the system that prevailed in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Within that system in Yugoslavia, the Secretariats for National Defence had the task of taking in military conscripts, that is to say, young men who reached a certain age when, due to their age, they got the status of a military conscript so to speak, that is to say, a person who is capable of taking part in the defence of the country. When records are made of such persons, that is to say, these young men, they were given a military speciality, that is to say, first of all, they had to undergo medical examinations, and then a certain commission would assign them a military speciality. That means a speciality that this soldier would engage in during their regular military service. So some went to armour units, others went to the navy, others went I don't know where, different arms and services.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, the Secretariat for National Defence sent these young men to do their military service when the time was right. And also, they received these soldiers when they returned to their home municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: When they would return from their military service, the Secretariats of National Defence had the task of assigning these military conscripts to certain reserve positions of reserve soldiers, junior officers, officers, et cetera, to certain units, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when this citizen, this young man who had been sent to do his military service would return to his home town, then the Secretariat and the municipality would assign him to the reserve force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This reserve could have meant an assignment in the Territorial Defence or in the reserve combat units of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not quite correct. Such a man could be assigned either to the reserve units or the JNA in the Territorial Defence but also they could be assigned work duty. That could also be their wartime assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So there were three categories: Work duty, reserve in the Territorial Defence or reserve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the basic difference between this reserve that we called the Territorial Defence and this other reserve which was the reserve force of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the vast majority of the army units were manned from the reserve force. This was not based on the territorial principle, that is to say, from several municipalities, military conscripts could have war assignments in a completely different municipality. While the Territorial Defence was established, it exclusively, upon the territorial principle, that is to say, that every municipality had its territorial units, at a given point in time, had the task of operating on the territory of their respective municipality only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to law and in real life -- we are talking about the period until the breakup of Yugoslavia -- who financed the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was financed by the municipalities that developed certain units on their territory. That is to say, the state budget, the republican budget, as far as I know, did not envisage any allocation for the Territorial Defence as was the case with the JNA. So it was the municipality, those social political communities that financed these units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, if I'm not mistaken, the law did envisage the obligation of the municipality to earmark certain minimal resources and to finance minimal reserve forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, another difference. Is it correct that the Territorial Defence had a relatively small skeleton organisation which, in case of imminent danger of war or war, heaven forbid, could increase by recruiting more men?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There was a skeleton organisation in every municipality. This was actually the Territorial Defence staff which, how should I put this, professionally worked on these jobs that were primarily administrative. So if need be, they would know what to do and how to do it in order to carry out full mobilisation so that it would be explained to the military conscripts where they should come, how they should do it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Territorial Defence staff, with this skeleton staff that they had, they had to have all the lists, plans, assignments, plans of mobilisation, plans of units, plans of commanders, et cetera, numerous elements so that at a given point in time, if necessary, they could actually organise and bring together this potential army of theirs?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence staff indeed had to have lists of all their units and members of their units. They also had to have records for each and every individual. They also had to have lists of the commanders and part of the mobilisation call-up papers or rather call-up papers only for part of the units in the Territorial Defence. The remainder was in the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. These soldiers, these young men who had done their service in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, when they would return to their municipalities, as you said, they would be assigned either to one of the two reserves or to the work duty units, and if they were assigned to the Territorial Defence or to this military reserve, as we call it, they were also issued certain equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Most of the members of the Territorial Defence were issued basic equipment, that is to say, that if it was possible for every individual to be equipped in that way, then a uniform would be bought for him and everything else that he needed. Yes, that is what they were issued then. If there was not enough, then people had to wait and priority was given to the purchase of uniforms, et cetera. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, of course [In English] ... we should be a little bit faster but if there is, I'm sure Mr. Jeffrey will tell me. [Interpretation] At any rate, if I understand you correctly, the point was for every soldier to be equipped, even when at home, with what was called basic equipment for a soldier and then when need be he could be called up to go wherever he was supposed to go?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, he did not have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked in the system for quite a long time. Was this the result of the lack of confidence on the part of the communist government that didn't really go that far, that didn't actually distribute weapons to the population?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't really think about this very much. I think that this was done for reasons of security, purely, so that weapons would not be abused by individuals because weapons are weapons. One kills with weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, thank you. We must add one more thing to this. I have to apologise, we did not directly mention this in the summaries that we have provided. Also the defence system in companies and also weapons that were there, can you tell us about this in a word or two.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all major companies, all major companies, in particular, developed within the Territorial Defence, their own units as well. They were organically linked to the Territorial Defence which would, in a given situation, be used for the defence of those companies as well. These companies that worked well would obtain their own equipment, equipment for their own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, just as the municipality had financed the Territorial Defence of the municipality, then the company, again, according to law, had to finance, at least a bigger company, had to finance its own defence within the enterprise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was true irrespective of whether this was a company of special interest to the state, for example, like your SPS that manufactured inter alia things that were used by the military. All major enterprises had to do that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every man of a certain age was a military conscript; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, unless he was ill or something like that, yes. This was established by special medical commissions, that is to say, whether they were able or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So let's just go through the way that mobilisation was carried out. I'm just going to put questions to you and you please just answer yes or no. Mobilisation could have been general or partial according to plans; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to the way it was carried out, it could be public or secret; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Territorial Defence, you worked your way up to commander for operations and teaching.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a small -- I have a small correction. I was assistant commander for training and education activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I do apologise. It was a pretty high post, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In the Territorial Defence headquarters, there were eight to ten employees. There weren't really high posts there, but -- well, perhaps one could say that assistant commander was a bit higher than the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before the outbreak of the war -- I'm referring to the general war in Bosnia, that is to say, the Serb aggression primarily, in 1991 -- the Territorial Defence command in Vitez, the commander was Mr. Hakija Cengic in Vitez; wasn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he leave the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was an ethnic Muslim, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when he was appointed commander of Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: He was appointed after the first multi-party elections that were held in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when the parties that won the largest number of votes divided these positions within the municipality amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to put a few questions to you related to the Galeb action. Would you agree with a general assessment present in the public, amongst the public in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, except in Serbia, that actually, just before the war broke out in 1989 and 1990, Serbia, as the most powerful republic, was preparing for a war against the other republics in an attempt to keep them in the Federation by force, and to that end certain measures were taken. One of these measures is the Galeb action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the Galeb action? Can you explain this to us, or to the Court, but as briefly as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: The Galeb action meant taking away the weapons of the Territorial Defence, and storing these weapons and mining and explosive devices in warehouses under JNA control. That would be it. The briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that until then the Territorial Defence had their own warehouses and their own weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now it was ordered that these weapons in the possession of the Territorial Defence be transferred to warehouses that were under army control?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in that way the Territorial Defence could no longer get their own weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: For a short period of time, the commission from the Territorial Defence headquarters could only see whether these weapons were still in these warehouses, but they could not be taken out. These weapons could not be taken back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of your professional opinion -- I'm asking you now because of the job you held -- did this significantly weaken the Territorial Defence? In this way, did the Yugoslav People's Army cripple the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This entire action was carried out through secret orders that were issued orally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even the president of the municipality was not informed about this. I'm talking about municipalities in general. And presidents of municipalities ex officio were presidents of war counsels for national defence that existed in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. We were told that we were not supposed to inform them about this either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were certainly an eyewitness of all of this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if necessary, you can explain this, even if there are some questions about this?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, and all of this happened in May 1990, the whole action went a step further. And then weapons were taken away from companies as well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to give you some documents so that you can have a look at them and see whether you know about that part of the action. I'm asking the usher to help me with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with this in the morning since we've got an ex parte hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will have that in the morning on the desks to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now, at least the main part of the hearing. Major Sajevic, would you be back, please, tomorrow morning to conclude your evidence. Don't speak to anybody about it until it's over, and that includes members of the Defence team. Very well. We'll adjourn now for the ex parte hearing. We'll sit again in 10 minutes for that. The main trial is adjourned until tomorrow morning, half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
